30:6.text: Little children, it is the last time: and as ye have heard that antichrist shall come, even now are there many antichrists; whereby we know that it is the last time.

provenance.other: “Antichrist” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, all Johannine: 1 John 2:18, 2:22, 4:3 and 2 John 1:7. The word appears nowhere else in the Bible, and the Book of Mormon uses it here and at 30:12 only. The 1830 sets it as the hyphenated, capitalised “Anti-Christ”.
provenance.significance: The term is not a label the chapter picks up loosely; the definition follows it. 1 John 2:22 asks “Who is a liar but he that denieth that Jesus is the Christ? He is antichrist,” and Alma 30:12 says of Korihor exactly that: “he began to preach unto the people, that there should be no Christ.” 1 John 2:18 adds the eschatological frame — “it is the last time … even now are there many antichrists” — and Korihor is introduced as one man in a series, the third such figure in this record after Sherem and Nehor. The chapter is not calling him a villain; it is placing him in a Johannine category and then testing him against its definition.

30:6.note: “And he was Anti-Christ, for he began to preach unto the people against the prophecies which had been spoken by the prophets, concerning the coming of Christ.” A KJV word confined to four verses of one author, imported with its definition attached: what makes a man antichrist in 1 John is the denial that Jesus is the Christ, and that is precisely the content of Korihor's preaching as verse 12 states it.

30:8.text: And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.

provenance.other: “Choose you this day” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 24:15, and “whom ye will serve” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The Book of Mormon reproduces the whole clause with a single change, “choose ye” for the KJV's “choose you” — the 1830 and 1920 texts agree on it — and marks the borrowing outright: “For thus saith the Scripture.”
provenance.significance: This is one of the Book of Mormon's rare explicit citations of a biblical text as scripture, and what it cites the text for is startling. Joshua 24:15 is a covenant ultimatum: choose, and here is where my house stands. Alma 30:7-11 makes it the constitutional basis of religious liberty — there was no law against a man's belief, because Scripture says choose. Recover the source's context and the citation is doing something the source did not authorise, because Joshua's very next speech (24:19-20) tells the people they cannot serve the LORD, and that if they forsake him “he will turn and do you hurt, and consume you.” The chapter then makes Joshua's warning come true on the man whose freedom the verse has just guaranteed. The verse that protects Korihor is the verse that condemns him.

30:8.note: A near-verbatim eight-word quotation, flagged by the text itself as scripture, and the only place the Book of Mormon quotes Joshua. The one departure is 'ye' for 'you' in the imperative, which is the 1830's own habit and not a variant of any English Bible. 1 Nephi 7:15 was recorded as a formal echo of this verse with no shared wording; here the wording is all there.

30:15.text: Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.

provenance.other: “Evidence of things not seen” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:1. “Evidence” itself occurs in exactly six, five of them Jeremiah's deed of purchase at Jeremiah 32; Hebrews 11:1 is the only KJV verse in which the word means grounds for belief rather than a legal document.
provenance.significance: Korihor's case is Hebrews 11:1 read backwards, clause by clause. Hebrews defines faith as the substance of things hoped for: Korihor opens at 30:13 by calling that hope “a foolish and a vain hope.” Hebrews defines it as the evidence of things not seen: Korihor answers at 30:15, “ye cannot know of things which ye do not see.” And when Alma replies at 30:40, the word he uses is the one word of Hebrews 11:1 that the KJV uses in no other epistemological sense — “what evidence have ye that there is no God?” The debate is conducted inside a single KJV verse, with each speaker holding one of its terms. Alma 32:21 then restores the verse whole, which is why that passage reads as an answer to this one rather than a new topic.

30:15.note: “Ye cannot know of things which ye do not see; therefore ye cannot know that there shall be a Christ.” No long run is shared, and the row is an allusion on the conceptual axis for that reason; but the three terms Korihor and Alma contest across verses 13, 15 and 40 — hope, sight, evidence — are the three terms of Hebrews 11:1, in Hebrews' own order, and 'evidence' in this sense is peculiar to that verse in the KJV. Adjudicated here rather than at Alma 32:21, which is the same verse quoted directly and at first sight the more obvious home, because this is its first use in the book and because the later passage only makes sense as a reply to this one.

30:22.text: And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?

provenance.other: “Pervert the right ways of the Lord” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 13:10, and “wilt thou not cease” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. “Seeking some to lead him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 13:11.
provenance.significance: Alma 10:28 already drew on Acts 13:10, and ADJUDICATING §4 would ordinarily make this a repeat of the book's own formula. It is not, and the reason is the reason that ruling allows for: at Alma 30 the passage the phrase came from is being enacted, not merely quoted. Acts 13:6-12 runs — a sorcerer and false prophet who withstood them (13:8); the charge, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord (13:10); the sentence, thou shalt be blind, pronounced by the apostle (13:11); the immediate affliction, and the man going about seeking some to lead him by the hand (13:11); the onlookers believing (13:12). Alma 30 runs the same sequence with one substitution — dumbness for blindness: Korihor withstood the truth (30:53), is charged with perverting the ways of the Lord (30:22, 30:60), is sentenced by Alma (30:47), is struck immediately (30:50), goes about from house to house begging (30:56), and the people are all converted (30:58). The Book of Mormon's set-piece confrontation with an unbeliever is the KJV's, with the affliction changed to fit a man whose offence was his mouth.

30:22.note: “Why do ye go about perverting the ways of the Lord?” The chapter opens and closes on this charge — verse 22 in the high priest's mouth, verse 60 in the narrator's — and the KJV has the phrase once, in Paul's rebuke of Elymas. What makes this a fresh link rather than a recurrence of Alma 10:28 is that the whole of Acts 13:6-12 is present here in order, which is not true anywhere else in the book; the phrase has returned to its source rather than recurring as a formula. Held at high: no single run is long, and the case rests on the sequence, which is why the subtype is type-scene.

30:23.text: But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence.

provenance.other: “Usurp authority” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Timothy 2:12. The verb 'usurp' appears nowhere else in the KJV in any form.
provenance.alternative: 'Usurp authority' had become ordinary English by 1830 and may owe nothing to the KJV.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one usurpation is a usurpation of the right to teach — “I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man” — and Korihor's charge is that the priests have usurped authority in order to teach: “laid down by ancient priests, to usurp power and authority over them, to keep them in ignorance.” Both verses treat teaching and authority as the same possession. Korihor is arguing, in the KJV's only vocabulary for the offence, that the whole priesthood stands where 1 Timothy says no one may stand.

30:23.note: “To usurp power and authority over them, to keep them in ignorance.” The KJV uses 'usurp' once, and the collocation with 'authority' is that verse's. Held at moderate rather than high because the phrase had independent currency in 1830 English and because only two words are shared; the rarity count is what keeps the row on the page.

30:25.text: The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.

provenance.route: Ezekiel 18:20 (with Deuteronomy 24:16) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “The son shall not bear” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 18:20. Deuteronomy 24:16 states the same principle judicially — “every man shall be put to death for his own sin” — and is repeated at 2 Kings 14:6 and 2 Chronicles 25:4. Alma 30:25 paraphrases rather than quotes: “a child is not guilty because of its parents.”
provenance.significance: Read alongside verse 8, this is the chapter's most easily missed structural fact: Korihor argues from the Bible, and the catalogue should say so. Twice in eighteen verses the Nephite dissenter's position rests on an Old Testament text — Joshua 24:15 licensing freedom of belief at verse 8, and Ezekiel 18's doctrine of individual guilt overturning inherited transgression here. Ezekiel 18 was itself written against a proverb about children's teeth set on edge by their fathers' grapes, which is exactly the shape of the doctrine Korihor is attacking. He is not an atheist improvising; he is quoting the prophets against the priests.

30:25.note: “Ye say that this people is a guilty and a fallen people, because of the transgression of a parent. Behold, I say that a child is not guilty because of its parents.” No wording is reproduced, which caps this at moderate, but the doctrine is stated in the KJV twice and only twice — Ezekiel 18:20 and the judicial rule of Deuteronomy 24:16 — and the Book of Mormon's sentence is a fair paraphrase of the first. What argues for dependence is that Korihor's other appeal, four verses earlier, is a verbatim scriptural quotation.
30:25.whyNot: Nothing verbal survives; the objection that a child should not answer for a parent is available to anyone and needs no source.

30:28.text: For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.

provenance.other: “Unknown God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 17:23, where it is the inscription on the Athenian altar. The Book of Mormon uses the phrase twice in this chapter, at 30:28 in Korihor's accusation and at 30:53 in the devil's commission to him.
provenance.significance: Korihor's charge is the Areopagus in reverse. Paul tells the Athenians that the god they worship ignorantly is the one he now declares; Korihor tells the Nephites that the being they fear is “some unknown being, which they say is God … which never hath been seen nor known.” Alma's answer at 30:44 then follows Paul's: the God who is not seen is known from what he made — Acts 17:24-28's argument from creation and providence, which Alma states as “all things denote there is a God … even the earth, and all things that is upon the face of it, yea, and its motion; yea, and also all the planets which move in their regular form.” Both speakers of this chapter have their lines from Acts 17, and Alma has Paul's.

30:28.note: “That they should … offend some unknown being, which they say is God; a being which never hath been seen nor known.” A KJV singleton, put into the mouth of the objector rather than the preacher, and answered four verses later by the natural theology that answers it in Acts 17. The devil's own words at 30:53 repeat the phrase — “they have all gone astray after an unknown God” — which is what raises the row above a single verbal coincidence.

30:31.text: For when they speak great swelling words of vanity, they allure through the lusts of the flesh, through much wantonness, those that were clean escaped from them who live in error.

provenance.other: “Great swelling words” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Peter 2:18 and Jude 1:16, which are parallel passages about the same subject. The Book of Mormon has the phrase exactly.
provenance.significance: The KJV's two occurrences both belong to its set descriptions of the false teacher, and 2 Peter 2 supplies the rest of Korihor's portrait in advance: teachers who bring in “damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them” (2:1), who “through covetousness … with feigned words make merchandise of you” (2:3), who “speak evil of the things that they understand not” (2:12), and who promise liberty while being “the servants of corruption” (2:19). Korihor denies the Christ, accuses the priests of merchandising, reviles, and offers a people he calls enslaved their freedom. The chapter has taken its antagonist's whole vocabulary from the epistle's chapter on antagonists — and it lets him accuse the priests of the covetousness 2 Peter 2:3 charges to him.

30:31.note: “And he did rise up in great swelling words before Alma, and did revile against the priests and teachers.” A three-word run confined in the KJV to two parallel verses, arriving in the sentence that formally classifies Korihor as a false teacher. Held at high because the surrounding portrait tracks 2 Peter 2 well beyond the borrowed phrase, and because the very accusation he makes is the one 2 Peter 2:3 makes against his own type.

30:32.text: For ye remember, brethren, our labour and travail: for labouring night and day, because we would not be chargeable unto any of you, we preached unto you the gospel of God.

provenance.other: The individual phrases here are not rare; what is rare is the argument's shape. 1 Thessalonians 2:5-9 is the KJV's fullest defence of a preacher against the charge of preaching for profit, and it runs: no flattering words, no cloke of covetousness, no glory sought of men, no burden laid on you, and labour night and day so as not to be chargeable. Alma 30:32-35 runs the same list in the same order. The single KJV rarity in the neighbourhood, “flattering words”, occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Thessalonians 2:5, and surfaces in this same speech at verse 47. Paul's own key word for the refusal of support, “chargeable”, occurs in exactly five KJV verses, three of them his (2 Corinthians 11:9, 1 Thessalonians 2:9, 2 Thessalonians 3:8).
provenance.significance: The accusation Korihor makes at 30:31 — that the priests preach “for the sake of glutting in the labors of the people” — is the standing ancient charge against itinerant preachers, and 1 Thessalonians 2 is the KJV's standing answer to it. Alma does not construct a defence; he gives Paul's, item by item, down to working with his own hands for his support. Recovering the source shows how completely the chapter has cast its protagonist as an apostle under attack: Korihor speaks 2 Peter 2's false teacher, Alma answers in 1 Thessalonians 2's.

30:32.note: “I have labored even from the commencement of the reign of the Judges, until now, with mine own hands, for my support.” Held at moderate because the wording is the Book of Mormon's own and the case rests on the order of the argument rather than on a run. Note that 1 Corinthians 4:12's 'working with our own hands' is already adjudicated in this book at Alma 1:3 and is registered as an exclusion at this verse; the row here is for the larger Thessalonian defence, of which the manual labour is one item and the refusal of flattering words at verse 47 another.

30:42.text: And the LORD said unto him, Wherewith? And he said, I will go forth, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets. And he said, Thou shalt persuade him, and prevail also: go forth, and do so.

provenance.other: “Lying spirit” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — 1 Kings 22:22, 22:23 and their doublets at 2 Chronicles 18:21, 18:22 — and all four belong to a single episode, Micaiah's vision of the heavenly council before Ahab's last battle.
provenance.significance: The relocation is the finding. In the KJV the lying spirit is a member of the LORD's own court who volunteers to deceive Ahab's prophets, and the text says so twice without embarrassment: “the LORD hath put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these thy prophets.” Alma 30:42 keeps the phrase and reassigns the agency — “thou art possessed with a lying spirit … but the Devil hath power over you” — and verse 53 completes the reassignment by having the deceiving spirit appear as an angel. The Book of Mormon takes the KJV's one term for prophetic deception and detaches it from the divine council, which is a doctrinal move made entirely by where the phrase is put.

30:42.note: “Thou art possessed with a lying spirit.” The KJV's only phrase for a spirit that makes a prophet speak falsely, drawn from the one episode that uses it. Alma applies to a false prophet what 1 Kings applies to the four hundred, and assigns to the devil what 1 Kings assigns to the LORD.

30:44.text: Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God, as ye tempted him in Massah.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 6:16 → Matthew 4:7 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Tempt the Lord your God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 6:16; “tempt the Lord thy God” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 4:7 and Luke 4:12, which quote it. Alma 30:44 reads “will ye tempt your God?” — the plural possessive of the Old Testament against the singular of both New Testament quotations.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 4:7 alone, with the pronoun adjusted to Alma's plural address, would explain the line without any Deuteronomic route.
provenance.significance: The two criteria pull apart here, and that is worth recording rather than resolving away. The wording is Deuteronomy's: 'your God', not 'thy God'. The situation is Matthew's, and unmistakably so — in Matthew 4:5-7 the tempter demands a demonstration of divine power, Jesus refuses to supply it, and this is the sentence he refuses with. That is Alma 30:43-44 exactly: Korihor asks for a sign to prove God has power, and Alma answers with this line before arguing that the signs are already given. So the route runs through Matthew, and the pronoun does not follow it.

30:44.note: “Thou hast had signs enough; will ye tempt your God?” Recorded as OT-via-NT on the situation rather than the wording, which is the reverse of the usual test and is flagged as such. tools/mediation-check.py could not decide the case: it found no divergence between Deuteronomy 6:16 and Matthew 4:7 at any point the Book of Mormon reproduces, and the pronoun that does discriminate is a single common word of the kind the tool deliberately ignores (ADJUDICATING §4). Read by eye, the possessive is Deuteronomy's; read by scene, the borrowing is Matthew's.
30:44.whyNot: Only three words are shared with either candidate, and 'tempt God' is a commonplace. A reader could take the line as an unmediated recollection of Deuteronomy and drop the Matthean route entirely.

30:46.text: And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.

provenance.other: “Grieved for the hardness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 3:5. The Book of Mormon's standing formula is 'hardness of heart' alone, which is adjudicated in this book at Alma 13:4; the element added here is the grieving, and it is the element that completes the KJV singleton.
provenance.significance: Mark 3:5 is Jesus in the synagogue looking round on his opponents “with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts” — a rare notice of what the KJV's Jesus feels in the moment before a miracle that his opponents will use against him. Alma 30:46 puts the same grief in the same position: it is the last thing said before the sign is given, and the sign destroys the man who asked for it. The borrowing carries Mark's discomfort into a passage that would otherwise read as simple judgment.

30:46.note: “Behold, I am grieved because of the hardness of your heart.” Written as a link rather than filed as a repeat of Alma 13:4, and the reason should be stated plainly because ADJUDICATING §4 makes the repeat the default within a book: Alma 13:4 rests on 'hardness of their hearts', which is the Book of Mormon's own formula, whereas this verse adds 'grieved', and grieving over hardness is what makes Mark 3:5 a singleton. The recurrence list points back so a reader can see both. A cautious editor could file this at Alma 13:4 instead.

30:47.text: For neither at any time used we flattering words, as ye know, nor a cloke of covetousness; God is witness:

provenance.other: “Flattering words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Thessalonians 2:5: “For neither at any time used we flattering words, as ye know, nor a cloke of covetousness; God is witness.”
provenance.significance: The singleton lands on Korihor, and it lands from the passage Alma has been answering him out of since verse 32. Paul's sentence pairs flattering words with a cloke of covetousness, and Korihor's accusation against the priests was precisely covetousness — that they glut themselves on the labours of the people. Alma returns both halves of 1 Thessalonians 2:5 to their author: the covetousness he has already disclaimed at 30:33, the flattering words he now assigns to Korihor. What the source says a true preacher never uses is what the false one is destroyed for.

30:47.note: “By thy lying and by thy flattering words.” A KJV singleton, and the second borrowing from the same short paragraph of Paul in one speech — the self-support argument at 30:32-35 is 1 Thessalonians 2:6-9, and this is 2:5. Mosiah 11:7 adjudicated the phrase first, in another book and of Noah's people; here it is doing different work, as the charge in a sentence of judgment.

30:47.text: And, behold, thou shalt be dumb, and not able to speak, until the day that these things shall be performed, because thou believest not my words, which shall be fulfilled in their season.

provenance.other: “Not able to speak” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:20, and “a writing table” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:63. Struck dumbness as a punishment occurs in the Bible once, in this episode.
provenance.significance: The KJV has exactly one man struck dumb, and the reason given is the reason given here: “because thou believest not my words.” Korihor's offence is stated in the same terms four verses earlier — he will not believe, and demands a sign instead. What settles the borrowing is what happens next. Zacharias, unable to speak, is handed a writing table and writes (Luke 1:63); Alma 30:51-52 has the chief judge “put forth his hand and wrote unto Korihor,” and Korihor “put forth his hand, and wrote.” The whole exchange that produces Korihor's confession — the most important speech in the chapter — is conducted in the one KJV episode where dumbness forces a man to write.

30:47.note: “God shall smite thee, that thou shalt become dumb, that thou shalt never open thy mouth any more.” Two KJV singletons and a shared cause of judgment, followed at 30:51-52 by the writing that Luke 1:63 requires. Subtype type-scene rather than close-verbal because the strongest evidence is the sequence — sentence for unbelief, dumbness, written exchange — rather than any run of words.

30:48.text: Then said Jesus unto him, Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe.

provenance.other: “Except ye see signs” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 4:48 — “Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe.” “Seeketh after a sign” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 12:39 and 16:4, which supply the judgment on the demand rather than its form.
provenance.significance: John 4:48 is a rebuke put as a conditional, and Korihor turns it into his own confession of terms: “except ye shew me a sign, I will not believe.” He states as his position the sentence Jesus states as an indictment, which is the chapter's method throughout — Korihor speaks the New Testament's descriptions of unbelief in the first person. Recovering John 4 supplies the outcome as well: the sign is given, the nobleman believes, and his whole house with him. Alma 30:58 has the same ending with the same word — “they were all converted again unto the Lord” — except that the man who asked is not among them.

30:48.note: “And except ye shew me a sign, I will not believe.” The KJV states this conditional once and states it as a reproach; Korihor adopts it as a demand, changing only 'see' to 'shew' and dropping the wonders. Held at high: the run is short but the sentence is verbatim in structure, and the KJV has no other verse of this shape.

30:53.text: And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.

provenance.other: “An angel of light” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 11:14. The Book of Mormon here has “in the form of an angel” rather than the full phrase, but the proposition — that the devil appears as an angel in order to deceive — is that verse's alone in the KJV.
provenance.significance: 2 Corinthians 11:13-15 is about false apostles “transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ,” and Paul's point is that the disguise is the method: “no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.” Korihor's confession supplies the mechanism the chapter has been withholding — he was not a cynic but a man who “verily believed” his own preaching, because the being who commissioned him looked like the being who commissions prophets. Recovering Paul's context makes the confession an argument rather than an excuse: this is exactly how, according to the KJV, false teaching gets itself believed by its own teachers.
provenance.alternative: 2 Nephi 9:9 adjudicated the phrase first and could be the proximate model, since the Book of Mormon has by now established the idea in its own words.

30:53.note: “For he appeared unto me in the form of an angel, and said unto me, Go and reclaim this people.” The KJV's one statement that Satan appears as an angel, applied to a commission that reads like a prophetic call. Written as a fresh link rather than a recurrence of 2 Nephi 9:9 because that is another book and another voice, and because here the claim is narrated as an event rather than asserted as doctrine.

30:53.text: Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.

provenance.other: “Carnal mind” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 8:7: “Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.”
provenance.significance: Korihor's explanation of his own success is Romans 8:7 used as a marketing analysis — “I taught them, because they were pleasing unto the carnal mind.” The source verse says why that would work: the carnal mind is not merely inclined against God but constitutionally incapable of subjection to him. Korihor has correctly identified the audience the KJV says exists, and his own final sentence, that he was deceived into believing his own doctrine, shows him to have been in it.

30:53.note: “And I taught them, because they were pleasing unto the carnal mind.” A KJV singleton, adjudicated first at Mosiah 16:5 in another book; the row is written here because the phrase does something new — it is the false teacher's own account of why his doctrine sold.

30:53.text: Now as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, so do these also resist the truth: men of corrupt minds, reprobate concerning the faith.

provenance.other: “Resist the truth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Timothy 3:8. “Withstood” occurs in exactly six, of which two matter here: 2 Timothy 3:8, where Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, and Acts 13:8, where Elymas the sorcerer withstood Paul and Barnabas. Alma 30:53's “I withstood the truth” fuses the verb of the one with the object of the other — and 2 Timothy 3:8 holds both in a single sentence.
provenance.significance: 2 Timothy 3:8's comparison is to Pharaoh's magicians, the KJV's type of the sign-worker who opposes a prophet with signs of his own, and the verse's judgment on them is that they are “men of corrupt minds, reprobate concerning the faith” — deceived, not merely dishonest, which is what Korihor confesses to being. Together with the Elymas sequence catalogued at 30:22, this puts Korihor at the junction of the KJV's two named magician-opponents. The Book of Mormon's word for what he did is the word both passages use.

30:53.note: “And for this cause, I withstood the truth, even until I have brought this great curse upon me.” Neither KJV verse has this exact phrase; 2 Timothy 3:8 has both of its halves within one sentence, and Acts 13:8 — whose scene this chapter has been running since verse 22 — has the verb applied to a sorcerer. Held at moderate because the fusion is the Book of Mormon's own.
